title: Role of omentin-1 in the global proteome of porcine pituitary cells: anti-proliferative and anti-apoptotic effects
projectDescription:
Background: The anterior pituitary plays a crucial role in endocrine regulation and homeostasis by orchestrating hormonal signaling, cellular growth, and functional adaptations. Adipokines regulate hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis influencing hormone secretion and cellular processes. Omentin-1, an adipokine primarily expressed in visceral adipose tissue, is involved in metabolic and reproductive functions. However, its role in pituitary remains unknown. We hypothesize that omentin-1 modulates protein abundance in pituitary cells. This study aimed to investigate role of omentin-1 in regulating key pathways in anterior pituitary cells of pigs with different metabolic statuses: normal-weight Large White pigs and genetically obese Meishan pigs. Results: High-throughput proteomic analysis of porcine anterior pituitary cells exposed to omentin-1 revealed 230 differentially abundant proteins (30 downregulated and 3 upregulated in Large White pigs, as well as 107 downregulated and 90 upregulated in Meishan pigs), associated with 116 gene ontology terms. The most significantly altered proteins were associated with cell cycle and DNA replication, gene expression regulation and posttranscriptional/posttranslational modifications. Apoptotic and proliferative mechanisms varied between breeds, suggesting different metabolic adaptation strategies. In Large White pigs, CDK5RAP2 and SIX1 played a key role in transcriptional and proliferative regulation, whereas in Meishan pigs, stronger proliferative control was linked to AKT1S1 and RHOA.  Moreover, Meishan pigs demonstrated a more dynamic regulation of apoptotic pathways (HTRA2, PARP2, DFFA), which may promote greater metabolic plasticity and better adaptation to physiological fluctuations. Additional in vitro experiments in Large White pigs showed that omentin-1 influenced key proliferative and apoptotic markers, downregulating cyclins D1, E1, A2, and B1, as well as caspase-3, while upregulating the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2, leading to an increased BCL2/BAX ratio. Further, omentin-1 modulated phosphorylation of selected kinases, including ERK1/2, AKT, AMPKα, and STAT3, in a time-dependent manner. It is also increased insulin receptor expression and promoted packaging and transport of secretory proteins. Conclusions: Proteomic and functional analyses revealed that omentin-1 regardless of breed exerts anti-proliferative and anti-apoptotic effects on porcine anterior pituitary cells, modulating key signaling pathways. These findings highlight that omentin-1 is a potential metabolic regulator influencing anterior pituitary function.

Project title: OMENTIN1 as a new regulator of female reproduction – expression and role in the pituitary–ovary axis. Study on swine model at different metabolic status.
sampleProcessingProtocol: The study used mature pigs of two breeds at the age of 5–8 months: normal-weight LW (91.76 ± 8.2 kg) and MS (30.62 ± 5.8 kg), which are characterized by greater backfat thickness. Pituitary glands were collected from pigs in the middle luteal phase (days 10-12, fully functional corpora lutea), which was evaluated based on ovarian morphology and the plasma profiles of estradiol and progesterone.  In vitro cultures were performed on AP cells from pooled AP glands. Each AP gland was extracted, divided into 1-2 mm thick pieces and isolated in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM; Sigma-Aldrich) supplemented with 0.1% BSA (BioShop) and antibiotic mixtures (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Single-cell suspensions were prepared by repeated tissue digestion with 0.2% type V collagenase (Sigma-Aldrich) and/or 0.25% pancreatin (Sigma-Aldrich) in DMEM for 10 min at 37 °C. After several centrifugation cycles (170 x g for 10 min), the AP cells were filtered through a 70 μm nylon mesh. The cells were cultured in McCoy's 5A medium supplemented with 10% horse serum (Sigma-Aldrich) and a 1% antibiotic mixture. The medium was further supplemented with 0.1% minimum essential medium (MEM) vitamins (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 0.01% MEM nonessential amino acids (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The cells were cultured in 6- or 96-well plates at densities of 1.5 × 106 and 10 × 104 cells per well, respectively. The AP cells were preincubated for 72 h at 37 °C in a water-saturated atmosphere of 5% CO2 and 95% air. Next, AP cells were cultured in McCoy's 5A medium supplemented with 1% horse serum or 1% horse serum with the examined substances in different experimental setups for 24, 48, or 72 h. Cells obtained from LW pigs were treated with OMNT1 (10, 50, 100 ng/mL), GnRH (100 ng/mL), or OMNT1 (10, 50 ng/mL) in combination with GnRH (100 ng/mL) and with pharmacological inhibitors for ERK1/2, AKT, AMPKα, STAT3, and INSR: PD098059 (Tocris), LY294002 (Cell Signaling Technology), Dorsomorphin (Sigma-Aldrich), AG490 (Sigma-Aldrich), and S961 (Phoenix Pharmaceuticals), respectively, depending on the experimental setup. After 24 h of incubation with the examined substances, the cells were stored at -70 °C. For protein isolation, cell lysis buffer (20% TFE (Sigma-Aldrich) in 100 mM TAEB (Sigma-Aldrich)) was added. After removing the medium, cells were treated with lysis buffer (50 µl per well) and harvested. The lysates were mixed and incubated on a thermoblock at 60 °C for 30 min. In addition, the samples were sonicated for 45 min in an ultrasonic bath. Samples were stored at -70 °C for further analysis.  Samples were digested using SP3 method with minor adjustments. Resulting peptide solutions were transferred to new tubes, and the resin was washed with 40 µL of 1% dimethyl sulfoxide and then with 60 µL of water. Peptide concentrations in pooled eluates were measured with Pierce Quantitative Colorimetric Peptide Assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific). 15 µg of peptides in 110 µL of 100 mM TEAB buffer was labeled with TMTpro 16plex tags (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in 40 µL ACN for 1 h on a vortex. The reaction was quenched with 8 µL of 5% hydroxylamine. Peptides were combined and desalted using four 30 mg Oasis HLB columns (Waters, Poland). The eluates were pooled, dried in a SpeedVac, resuspended in 500 µL of 10 mM ammonium hydroxide with 2% ACN, and used for high-pH offline fractionation. Peptides were separated using HpRP chromatography on an XBridge Peptide BEH C18 column (4.6 x 250 mm, 130 Å, 5 µm; Waters, Poland) at a flow rate of 0.8 mL/min over 50-mins on a Waters Acquity UPLC H-class system. Mobile phases included water (A), ACN (B), and 100 mM ammonium hydroxide (C), with phase C maintained at 10% throughout the gradient. Fraction collection commenced at the 2-minute mark, with one fraction collected every minute. A total of 48 fractions were collected, dried in a SpeedVac, and reconstituted in Evosep solvent A (0.1% FA in water) with 30 min of mixing, followed by sonication. Fractions 1-16 were pooled with fractions 33-48 by combining every 32nd fraction, whereas the middle fractions (17-32) were directly subjected to MS analysis. HpRP fractions were analyzed using an LC-MS system comprising of Evosep One (Evosep Biosystems) directly coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Samples were loaded onto disposable Evotips Pure C18 trap columns (Evosep Biosystems) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Peptide separation was carried out on an analytical column (Dr. Maisch C18 AQ, 1.9 µm beads, 150 µm ID, 15 cm length, Bruker) at a flow rate of 220 nl/min over 88 min using the Evosep Extended method. MS1 resolution was set to 60, 000, with a scan range of 300–1700 m/z. For MS2, the resolution was set at 30, 000. Dynamic exclusion was applied for 20 s. Precursors were fragmented in HCD mode with a normalized collision energy of 30%. TurboTMT resolution mode was set to 'TMTpro Reagents'.
dataProcessingProtocol: The raw data were processed using the MaxQuant/Andromeda suite (version 2.5) with the Sus scrofa reference proteome from UniProt (UP000008227, version 2021_01, one protein sequence per gene, 22788 sequences) supplemented with a contaminant database. The search parameters were as follows: enzyme - trypsin/P, fixed modifications - Methylthio (C), variable modifications - oxidation (M), quantification - TMTpro 16-plex (corrected according to Certificate of Analysis), and maximum missed cleavages set to 2. Peptide-spectrum match and protein false discovery rate, performed using a target/decoy strategy with a reversed database, were set to 0.01. Further data analysis was performed in Perseus (version 1.6.15). Proteins were identified by site, proteins from the reverse database, and potential contaminants were filtered out. Additionally, proteins lacking at least three values in at least one group were excluded, after which the signal was normalized to the loading factors. The data were then log2-transformed, and missing values were replaced using a normal distribution approach. The batch effect was removed using Limma. A two-sample t test was performed to identify DAPs between the treatment and control groups. Fold changes (FCs) of ≤ -1.2 or ≥ 1.2 were considered for further analyses to detect biological variation relevant to physiological processes.
